{{italic title}}
The '''Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act''' ('''DRIPA''') is a statute of the province of [[British Columbia]], Canada. Enacted in 2019, it establishes a legal commitment to uphold the principles of the [[United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples]] (UNDRIP) in provincial law and policy.<ref name="BCGov">{{cite web |title=Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/indigenous-people/new-relationship/united-nations-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples |publisher=Government of British Columbia |access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref><ref name="t669"/>

The Act makes British Columbia the first jurisdiction in Canada to legislate the implementation of UNDRIP, and forms a central component of the province's approach to reconciliation with Indigenous peoples.<ref name="ActionPlanIntro">{{cite web |title=Declaration Act Action Plan (Introduction) |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/government/ministries-organizations/ministries/indigenous-relations-reconciliation/declaration_act_action_plan.pdf |publisher=Government of British Columbia |access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref> It has become the subject of political controversy in British Columbia due to the legal uncertainty resulting from its implementation, including potential impacts on governance, [[private property rights]], and economic development.<ref name="l943"/><ref name="i754">{{cite web | last=Chan | first=Kenneth | title=B.C. First Nations threaten legal action over any weakening of DRIPA law | website=Daily Hive | date=2026-04-20 | url=https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/bc-first-nations-council-dripa-suspension-opposition-letter | access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>

== Background ==
The Act was introduced by Minister of Indigenous Relations and Reconciliation [[Scott Fraser (politician)|Scott Fraser]] under the [[British Columbia New Democratic Party|New Democratic Party]] government of Premier [[John Horgan]]. It was passed unanimously by the [[Legislative Assembly of British Columbia]] in November 2019.<ref name="ActionPlanIntro" /><ref>{{Cite news |last= |date=2019-11-26 |title=UN Indigenous rights bill approved unanimously in B.C. |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/b-c-first-nations-leaders-worry-u-n-indigenous-rights-bill-may-be-in-trouble-1.5374095 |access-date=2026-10-26 |work=[[CBC News]] |language=en-CA}}</ref> The legislation was conceived in response to advocacy from the [[Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada]] to adopt and implement UNDRIP as the framework for reconciliation.<ref name="BCGov" />

== Provisions ==
DRIPA mandates the British Columbia government to bring its laws in line with UNDRIP.<ref name="BCGov"/>
UNDRIP states that free, prior, and [[informed consent]] from Indigenous Peoples is required on matters affecting their rights, lands, territories, and resources.<ref name=H2022/><ref name="t669">{{cite web | title=What to know about DRIPA and why B.C. wants to amend the Indigenous rights law | website=The Globe and Mail | date=2026-04-21 | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-dripa-bc-indigenous-rights-law-eby/ | access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>
The province states that DRIPA does not grant First Nations a veto over resource development, although promises "redress and restitution" when consent is not granted.<ref>{{cite news | newspaper=CBC News | first=Tanya | last=Fletcher | title=From champion to target: B.C.'s premier faces a complicated road ahead to reconciliation: Wet'suwet'en protests mark John Horgan's first major test of province's historic Indigenous rights legislation | date=12 February 2020 | url= https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/from-champion-to-target-b-c-premier-faces-a-complicated-road-ahead-to-reconciliation-1.5461783 }}</ref><ref name=H2019>{{cite news | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | first=Justine | last=Hunter | title=B.C. introduces legislation to align its laws, policies with United Nations' Indigenous rights declaration | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/british-columbia/article-bc-introduces-legislation-to-align-its-laws-policies-with-united/ | date=25 October 2019 }}</ref><ref name=H2022>{{cite news | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | first=Justine | last=Hunter | title=Tahltan Nation has final say on proposed $600-million gold mine | url= https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/british-columbia/article-tahltan-nation-has-final-say-on-proposed-600-million-gold-mine/ | date=6 June 2022 }}</ref>

Key provisions include:

* '''Section 3''' requires the government to take all necessary measures to ensure provincial laws are consistent with UNDRIP, in consultation and cooperation with Indigenous peoples.<ref name="BCGov" /><ref name="Alignment">{{cite web |title=Alignment of Laws |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/indigenous-people/new-relationship/united-nations-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples/alignment-of-laws |publisher=Government of British Columbia |access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>
* '''Section 4''' mandates the development and implementation of an action plan, created jointly with Indigenous peoples, to achieve the objectives of the declaration.<ref name="BCGov" /><ref name="ActionPlan">{{cite web |title=Declaration Act Action Plan |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/indigenous-people/new-relationship/united-nations-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples/implementation |publisher=Government of British Columbia |access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>
* '''Section 5''' requires the government to report annually on progress toward aligning laws and implementing the action plan.<ref name="AnnualReport">{{cite web |title=Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act 2020/21 Annual Report |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/government/ministries-organizations/ministries/indigenous-relations-reconciliation/declaration_act_annual_report_2021.pdf |publisher=Government of British Columbia |access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>
* '''Sections 6 and 7''' allow the provincial cabinet (Executive Council), on behalf of the government, to negotiate and enter into agreements with Indigenous governing bodies.  Section 6 agreements are broader in nature.<ref name=DRIPA>{{cite web | title=Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act [SBC 2019] Chapter 44 | url=https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/19044 | publisher=King's Printer | author=Government of British Columbia }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Making Decisions Together | url= https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/indigenous-people/new-relationship/united-nations-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples/making-decisions-together | date=11 March 2026 | publisher=Province of British Columbia }}</ref>

== Implementation ==
When the legislation was passed in 2019, Minister Fraser told fellow [[MLAs]] that the act was intended as aspirational and to provide guidance.<ref name="c612"/>
The government said that the process of bringing its laws into alignment with UNDRIP would take decades.<ref name=EBGM>{{cite news | url= https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/editorials/article-bcs-reconciliation-agenda-needs-an-immediate-rewrite/ | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | date=11 April 2026 | author=The Editorial Board | title=B.C.'s reconciliation agenda needs an immediate rewrite }}</ref>
In March 2022, the Government of British Columbia released an action plan outlining 89 priority actions to be undertaken over five years, organized around themes including self-determination and Indigenous governance.<ref name="ActionPlan" /> To support implementation, the province established the Declaration Act Secretariat in 2022, a central agency responsible for coordinating the alignment of laws and policy across government.<ref name="Secretariat">{{cite web |title=Declaration Act Secretariat |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/indigenous-people/new-relationship/united-nations-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples/declaration-act-secretariat |publisher=Government of British Columbia |access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>

== Reception ==
The Act was praised by Indigenous advocacy groups upon passage, while critics argued it was unnecessary thanks to existing laws and did not effectively protect the rights of non-Indigenous third-party interests.<ref name="h925">{{cite web | last=Hastings | first=Hayley Woodin | title=Five years on, B.C.'s DRIPA sits in legal and political crosshairs | website=Business in Vancouver | date=2024-10-01 | url=https://www.biv.com/news/economy-law-politics/five-years-on-bcs-dripa-sits-in-legal-and-political-crosshairs-9597066 | access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>

==Land-use decision-making powers granted to Indigenous bodies under DRIPA==
An important aspect of DRIPA is that it allows the province to transfer land-use decision-making powers to indigenous governing bodies.<ref name=Bennett24>{{cite news | newspaper=Business in Vancouver | date=1 October 2024 | first=Nelson | last=Bennett | title=Five years on, B.C.'s DRIPA sits in legal and political crosshairs | url=https://www.biv.com/news/economy-law-politics/five-years-on-bcs-dripa-sits-in-legal-and-political-crosshairs-9597066 }}</ref> 
Early examples are agreements with the [[Tahltan First Nation|Tahltan]] and [[shíshálh Nation|shíshálh]] First Nations.
Other examples include a transfer to the [['Namgis First Nation]] of a large area of forest land on Vancouver Island; an agreement with the [[Tsilhqot'in]] in B.C.'s central interior concerning environmental assessment of mining projects; and the government is working on a land claim by the [[Kaska Nation|Kaska Dena]] to a region representing about 10% of B.C.'s total area.<ref name=Fletcher260131>{{cite news | first=Tom | last=Fletcher | title=BC gold mine sets path for independent nations: Tahltan Nation share of Eskay Creek includes Crown revenue share and tax-free jobs. | newspaper=Western Standard | url=https://www.westernstandard.news/opinion/fletcher-bc-gold-mine-sets-path-for-independent-nations/70818 | date=31 January 2026 }}</ref><ref name=Bennett24/><ref name=BC2022/>

===Tahltan decision-making agreements and proposals===
In June 2022, the first agreement under DRIPA was made with the [[Tahltan First Nation|Tahltan Central Government]].  
The agreement "honours Tahltan's jurisdiction in land-management decisions in Tahltan Territory", where the territory comprises a substantial 95,933 square kilometres in northwest B.C., equivalent to 11% of B.C.'s land area.<ref name=BC2022>{{cite web | title=Tahltan Central Government, B.C. make history under Declaration Act | date=6 June 2022 | publisher=BC Gov News | url=https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2022PREM0034-000899 }}</ref>
Most of the province's land base is subject to Indigenous land claims, and Premier [[John Horgan]] said the agreement aimed to reduce uncertainty for investors regarding environmental and land-use decisions.<ref name=Hunter220606>{{cite news | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | title=Tahltan Nation has final say on proposed $600-million gold mine | date=6 June 2022 | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/british-columbia/article-tahltan-nation-has-final-say-on-proposed-600-million-gold-mine/ | first=Justine | last=Hunter }}</ref>
Two further agreements were signed with the Tahltan in 2023 and 2026 under Section 7 of DRIPA regarding decisions under the ''Environmental Assessment Act'' relating to the Red Chris and Eskay Creek mines.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/oic/arc_oic/0348_2021 | title=Order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council No. 348 | date=15 June 2021  | publisher=Province of British Columbia }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2026ENV0003-000074 | title=Tahltan, B.C. make history with consent-based decisions on Eskay Creek mine | date=26 January 2026 | publisher=BC Gov News }}</ref><ref name=Garrett>{{cite news | first1=Catherine | last1=Garrett | first2=Caitrin | last2=Pilkington | newspaper=CBC News | title=Eskay Creek gold and silver mine in northwest B.C. gets green light | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/eskay-creek-gold-silver-mine-environmental-approval-9.7062257 | date=26 January 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | first1=Daniel | last1=Bornstein | first2=Kerry | last2=Kaukinen | first3=Rachael | last3=Carlson | first4=Rob | last4=Legge | title=Skeena Resources secures approval for C$318M Impact Benefit Agreement with Tahltan Nation | date=15 December 2025 | url= https://www.mccarthy.ca/en/experience/skeena-resources-secures-approval-for-c-318m-impact-benefit-agreement-with-tahltan-nation | publisher=McCarthy Tetrault }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | publisher=BC Gov News | title=Tahltan Nation, B.C. sign historic consent-based decision-making agreement | date=1 November 2023 | url=https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2023ENV0061-001707}}</ref>
These agreements mean the projects require consent of the Tahltan to proceed, and do not limit the terms under which consent can be withheld.<ref name=Hunter220606/><ref name=Hoekstra220621/> 
This may increase uncertainty for the project's proponent, and could reduce the predictability that the B.C. government argues will come with the agreements.<ref name=Hoekstra220621>{{cite web | url= https://cassels.com/insights/will-the-bc-tahltan-project-consent-agreement-deliver-on-its-promises/ | first=Arend | last=Hoekstra | title=Will the BC/Tahltan Project Consent Agreement Deliver on its Promises? | date=21 June 2022 | publisher=Cassels }}</ref>

Each First Nation's land-use agreement is unique, so industry stakeholders have expressed concern that there could be inconsistent land-use processes and decisions when a project overlaps two First Nation claim areas.<ref name=Brixton>{{cite web | title=Tahltan-BC Land Stewardship Planning Project: Fundamental Concerns with Consultation to-Date | date=22 December 2025 | publisher=Cassels.com | url=https://icbaindependent.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/LT-BC-re-Concerns-with-the-Tahltan-BC-Land-Stewardship-Planning-Project-22-Dec-202557.pdf }}</ref>
Also, under the planned ''Tahltan-BC Land Stewardship Planning Project'' (which covers 58,011 square kilometres of the Tahltan Territory), an investor in a new or existing project may have rules changed or tenure ended, leading to economic losses.<ref name=Gardner/><ref name=Stone>{{cite news | newspaper=National Post | first=Todd | last=Stone | title=B.C.'s DRIPA law should be fixed, not scrapped: B.C. does not need to choose between reconciliation and economic prosperity | date=3 May 2026 | url=https://nationalpost.com/opinion/b-c-s-dripa-law-should-be-fixed-not-scrapped }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://planninginpartnership.ca/p/60ae88e7636b3e002209775a/project-details?currentPage=1&pageSize=10&keywords=&projectTypes=&sortBy=-dateAdded&ms=1778275621969 | title=Tahltan-B.C. Land Stewardship Planning | publisher=Cassels Brock & Blackwell LLP }}</ref>
The President of the ''Independent Contractors and Businesses Association'' of B.C. says this risks making B.C. "un-investable".<ref name=Gardner>{{cite news | first=Chris | last=Gardner | title=Secret Eby government land-use deals are 'expropriation by stealth,' says business leader | url=https://northernbeat.ca/opinion/secret-eby-government-land-use-deals-are-expropriation-by-stealth-says-business-leader/ | date=9 January 2026 | newspaper=Northern Beat }}</ref>
Another concern is that the provincial government has granted exclusive decision-making power to the Tahltan over publicly-owned land in a large and mineral-rich region of B.C. based on a claim of Aboriginal title, when Aboriginal title has not been established under Canadian law.<ref>{{cite news | first=Warren | last=Mirko | title=Eby government gives Tahltan Nation veto over gold mine development | newspaper=Northern Beat | date=29 November 2025 | url= https://northernbeat.ca/opinion/eby-government-gives-tahltan-nation-veto-over-gold-mine-development/ }}</ref>

===''shíshálh'' decision-making agreements and proposals===
In 2022 the province began a process to negotiate an arrangement with the shíshálh (Sechelt) under Section 7 of DRIPA to manage dock leases and licences in an area along the [[Sunshine Coast, British Columbia|Sunshine Coast]], 50 kilometres northwest of [[Vancouver]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/oic/arc_oic/0444_2022 | title=Order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council No 444 | date=2 August 2022 | publisher=Province of British Columbia }}</ref><ref name=Hunter250225>{{cite news | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | title=B.C. government announces First Nations land pact on Sunshine Coast, months after deal was inked | first=Justine | last=Hunter | date=25 February 2025 | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-bc-government-announces-first-nations-land-pact-on-sunshine-coast/ }}</ref>
This generated concern among owners of private and commercial docks and boathouses, and in the summer of 2024, the government announced a resolution that effectively shields existing facilities from new rules imposed by the First Nation.<ref name=Hunter250225/><ref>{{cite web | title=Order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council No. 159 | publisher=Province of British Columbia | date=7 April 2025 | url=https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/oic/oic_cur/0159_2025 }}</ref>
On January 29, 2025 the B.C. government publicly announced a wider agreement that it had signed on August 16, 2024 to settle Aboriginal title with the [[shíshálh Nation]] over more than half a million hectares of the [[Sechelt Peninsula]].<ref name=Hunter250225/><ref>{{cite news | title=The B.C. NDP's pattern of secrecy, coverup and denial on Indigenous relations: Their agenda on Indigenous relations is so secretive, those in charge don't even tell their own people what they are doing and why | date=10 December 2025 | url= https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/vaughn-palmer-bc-ndp-david-eby-government-pattern-of-secrecy-coverup-denial-indigenous-relations | first=Vaughn | last=Palmer | newspaper=Vancouver Sun }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2025IRR0003-000057 | date=29 January 2025 | title=shíshálh Nation, B.C. renew landmark reconciliation agreement | publisher=BC Gov News }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url= https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/natural-resource-stewardship/consulting-with-first-nations/agreements/factsheet_shishalh_fa.pdf | date=6 March 2025 | title=shíshálh Nation – British Columbia Foundation Agreement Renewal Fact Sheet }}</ref>
The agreement also proposed, within five years, to pay $104 million for economic development and other programs and to reach an arrangement on exclusive decision-making by the shíshálh over matters that were not yet defined.<ref name=Hunter250225/><ref>{{cite web | url= https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/natural-resource-stewardship/consulting-with-first-nations/agreements/2024_foundation_agreement_renewal.pdf | title=Foundation Agreement Addendum Regarding Medium-Term Milestones }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=B.C. government defends withholding details of shíshálh Nation deal | first=Vaughn | last=Palmer | date=24 February 2025 | newspaper=Vancouver Sun | url=https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/bc-government-defends-withholding-details-of-shishalh-nation-deal }}</ref>

A group from the agreement area, the Pender Harbour Area Residents Association (PHARA), has filed a lawsuit to have DRIPA struck down, as they would be subject to decisions made by a governing body (the shíshálh Nation) for which they could not vote and which is not accountable to them, saying this violates democratic rights protected under section 3 of Canada's ''Charter of Rights and Freedoms''.<ref name=Bennett240514>{{cite news | first=Nelson | last=Bennett | date=14 May 2024 | title=DRIPA may face first legal test over boat docks | url=https://www.biv.com/news/economy-law-politics/dripa-may-face-first-legal-test-over-boat-docks-8740833 | newspaper=Business in Vancouver }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=DRIPA challenge filed in B.C. Supreme Court: On Feb.9, notice of civil claim was submitted by the Pender Harbour and Area Residents Association related its continued opposition to the province's Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. | first=Connie | last=Jordison | date=19 February 2026 | url=https://www.coastreporter.net/local-news/dripa-challenge-filed-in-bc-supreme-court-11890322 | newspaper=Coast Reporter }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | newspaper=National Post | title=Democracy can't exist in B.C. as long as DRIPA is around | first=Geoff | last=Russ | url=https://nationalpost.com/opinion/geoff-russ-democracy-cant-exist-in-b-c-as-long-as-dripa-is-around | date=7 May 2026 }}</ref>
Also, PHARA said Aboriginal rights defined in DRIPA and UNDRIP are inconsistent with Aboriginal rights described in Canadian law under section 35 of the ''Constitution Act, 1982'', particularly concerning the need under Canadian law to "reasonably balance" Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal interests regarding asserted but unproven Aboriginal land claims.<ref name=PHARAnotice/>{{rp|23–24}}<ref name=Bennett24/><ref>{{cite web | title=Recent deal highlights B.C. government's costly 'pay to play' approach to land use | date=21 February 2026 | first=Geoffrey | last=Moyse | url=https://www.fraserinstitute.org/commentary/recent-deal-highlights-bc-governments-costly-pay-play-approach-land-use | publisher=Fraser Institute}}</ref>
Additionally, PHARA wants the court to consider whether DRIPA goes beyond B.C.'s legal authority since the federal government holds exclusive jurisdiction of Indigenous rights in Canada, as indicated in sections 91(24) and 92 of the ''Constitution Act, 1867''.<ref name=PHARAnotice>{{cite web | url= https://mcmillanllp.sharefile.com/share/view/s103d1a984b8e474b8db23154b0b1e331 | title=Notice of Civil Claim | date=9 February 2026 }}</ref>{{rp|27–28}}<ref name=PHARA>{{cite news | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | title=Constitutional Challenge Filed Against BC's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/markets-news/Newsfi%E2%80%A6inst-bc-s-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-act-dripa/ | date=9 February 2026 }}</ref><ref name=Bennett240514/>

==Major legal cases that reference DRIPA==
The B.C. Supreme Court referred to DRIPA in its August 2025 decision in ''[[Cowichan Tribes v. Canada]]'' that granted Aboriginal title to the [[Cowichan Tribes]] on 732 acres in the city of [[Richmond, British Columbia|Richmond]].<ref>{{cite news | first=David | last=Ebner | date=10 August 2025 | title=Major land claims ruling says B.C. Indigenous group has claim to a portion of city and port lands | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-indigenous-cowichan-tribes-aboriginal-richmond-fraser/ | newspaper=The Globe and Mail }}</ref>  
In a first for Canada, Aboriginal title was established over privately-owned land, and Aboriginal title was declared a "prior and senior right" to private property title, creating uncertainty regarding the status and validity of private land titles.<ref>{{cite web | first=Bruce | last=Pardy | date=28 October 2025 | publisher=Fraser Institute | title=Eby bringing B.C. to its knees with Aboriginal land deals | url=https://www.fraserinstitute.org/commentary/eby-bringing-bc-its-knees-aboriginal-land-deals }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | author=Osler | title=The longest trial, a big impact: Cowichan's Aboriginal title victory | url=https://www.osler.com/en/insights/blogs/indigenous/aboriginal-title/ | date=14 October 2025 }}</ref><ref name="l943">{{cite web | last=DeRosa | first=Katie | title=B.C. premier says landmark court decision on DRIPA already having legal consequences | website=CBC | date=2026-04-09 | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-court-decision-dripa-9.7157088 | access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref><ref name="c612"/>

In December 2025, in a 2–1 decision, the [[British Columbia Court of Appeal]] reversed an earlier ruling regarding the [[Gitxaala Nation|Gitxaala]] lawsuit in ''[[Gitxaała v. British Columbia|Gitxaala v. British Columbia]]''.  The lawsuit challenged the province's automated online registry system that allowed prospecting and claims for [[mineral rights]] to be registered prior to consultation with the Gitxaala on public land where the Gitxaala had made a claim of Aboriginal title.<ref>{{cite news | newspaper=The Globe and Mail | first=Justine | last=Hunter | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-bc-to-amend-indigenous-rights-act-after-court-ruling-on-mineral-claims/ | title=B.C. to amend Indigenous rights act after court ruling on mineral claims | date=9 December 2026 }}</ref><ref name="c612"/><ref>{{cite web | title=Gitxaala First Nation Challenges British Columbia's Mineral Tenure Regime | first1=Robin | last1=Longe | first2=David | last2=Hunter | first3=Alexandra | last3=Edgar | date=24 May 2023 |publisher=Dentons | url= https://www.dentonsmininglaw.com/gitxaala-first-nation-challenges-british-columbias-mineral-tenure-regime/ }}</ref>
The court referred to B.C.'s ''Interpretation Act'' (a guide to interpreting provincial laws), which was changed in 2021 by then-attorney general David Eby to say "Every act and regulation must be construed as being consistent with" UNDRIP.<ref name=castanet/><ref>{{cite web | title=Interpretation Act | url=https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96238_ | date=31 March 2026 | author=bclaws.gov.bc.ca }}</ref>
As the ''Interpretation Act'' said "must" be consistent with UNDRIP, the court said "Properly interpreted", DRIPA incorporates UNDRIP into the positive law of British Columbia "with immediate legal effect".<ref name=EBGM/><ref name=castanet>{{cite news | newspaper=Castanet.net | date=20 April 2026 | title=Eby called changes to Indigenous law 'non-negotiable,' but series of backdowns ensued | url=https://www.castanet.net/news/BC/609873/Eby-called-changes-to-Indigenous-law-non-negotiable-but-series-of-backdowns-ensued }}</ref><ref name=Carman>{{cite news | newspaper=CBC News | date=24 April 2026 | title=How DRIPA drove the B.C. government to a crisis point: The consensus was the bill had no power to change laws. The courts disagreed | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-dripa-crisis-point-9.7175559 | first=Tara | last=Carman }}</ref>

==Proposals for changes to DRIPA==
Following the Gitxaala and Cowichan decisions, Premier [[David Eby]] vowed to appeal the rulings and amend DRIPA to reduce government liability and address legal uncertainty.  Since most B.C. laws had not yet been revised, any law that was not aligned with UNDRIP could be challenged so "Too much rides on it in terms of our province's prosperity."<ref name=ctv>{{cite news | newspaper=CTV News | title=Eby says DRIPA law could be amended after First Nations win appeal in mining case | date=5 December 2025 | url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/eby-says-dripa-law-could-be-amended-after-first-nations-win-appeal-in-mining-case/ }}</ref><ref name=EBGM/><ref>{{cite news | newspaper=Business in Vancouver | url=https://www.biv.com/news/premier-eby-says-changing-dripa-is-non-negotiable-and-will-be-pushed-into-law-12090739 | first=Wolfgang | last=Depner | date=1 April 2026 | title=Premier Eby says changing DRIPA is 'non-negotiable' and will be pushed into law }}</ref><ref name=derosa>{{cite news | newspaper=CBC News | title=B.C. premier says landmark court decision on DRIPA already having legal consequences: The Gitxaala decision has been the basis of the NDP's push to overhaul DRIPA | first=Katie | last=DeRosa | date=8 April 2026 | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-court-decision-dripa-9.7157088 }}</ref>
A [[The Globe and Mail|Globe and Mail]] editorial said amendments to DRIPA and the ''Interpretation Act'' would allow legislation to be aligned in an orderly way, since investors face "crippling uncertainty" over what laws govern B.C.<ref name=EBGM/>
Former federal Minister of Justice [[Jody Wilson-Raybould]] recommended a separate implementation act for aligning laws, since DRIPA's lack of an effective legislative mechanism regarding how UNDRIP is to be translated into Canadian law had caused "confusion and complexities for the courts".<ref name=JW>{{cite news | title=B.C.'s UNDRIP law was doomed from the start | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/article-bcs-undrip-law-was-doomed-from-the-start/ | first=Jody | last=Wilson-Raybould | date=22 April 2026 | newspaper=The Globe and Mail }}</ref>

In April 2026, Premier Eby announced that, although he remained convinced that the legal uncertainty needed to be addressed, he had reversed his decision to amend DRIPA due to opposition from First Nations and from within the NDP caucus, choosing instead to set up a joint working group with the First Nations Leadership Council to "find solutions" by the fall 2026 legislative session.<ref name="t669"/>

The opposition [[Conservative Party of British Columbia]] has said it would repeal DRIPA.<ref name="c612">{{cite web | last=Carman | first=Tara | title=How DRIPA drove the B.C. government to a crisis point | website=CBC | date=2026-04-24 | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-dripa-crisis-point-9.7175559 | access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref> In August 2026, Conservative MLA [[Harman Bhangu]] applied for an [[initiative petition]] that would repeal DRIPA.<ref name="g222">{{cite web | title=B.C. Conservative MLA makes move to repeal DRIPA | publisher=CBC | date=2026-08-27 | url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/harman-bhangu-initiative-petition-dripa-bc-9.7323111 | access-date=2026-08-28}}</ref> If the petition obtains signatures of 10 percent of voters in all 93 of B.C.'s electoral districts by 25 January 2027, the draft bill bill could be referred to the provincial legislature for a vote.<ref>{{cite news | newspaper=Victoria Times-Colonist | url=https://www.timescolonist.com/local-news/elections-bc-allows-petition-seeking-indigenous-laws-repeal-to-proceed-12716649 | first=Chuck | last=Chiang | date=27 August 2026 | title=Elections B.C. allows petition seeking Indigenous law's repeal to proceed: Even if the petition succeeds - it requires the signatures of 10 per cent of voters in all 93 of B.C.'s electoral districts by Jan. 25, 2027 - it is not binding }}</ref>

The [[Conservative Party of British Columbia]] won the [[2026 British Columbia general election]]. In an interview with [[Global News]] following the election, which saw a Conservative majority, Grand Chief [[Stewart Phillip]] described any attempt at repealing DRIPA by the government-elect as, "a declaration of war."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jung |first1=Angela |title=B.C. First Nations chief warns ripping up DRIPA is a ‘declaration of war’ |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/12121663/bc-first-nations-chief-warns-ripping-dripa-declaration-war/ |publisher=Global News |access-date=27 October 2026}}</ref> Phillip's late wife, [[Joan Phillip]], while an MLA for the [[British Columbia New Democratic Party|NDP]], had opposed her own party's suggestion to amend the act before she passed away.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Birnie |first1=Marissa |title=Will Penticton's Joan Phillip bring down the BC NDP government over DRIPA? |url=https://www.castanetkamloops.net/news/BC/608144/Will-Pentictons-Joan-Phillip-bring-down-the-BC-NDP-government-over-DRIPA |publisher=The Canadian Press |access-date=27 October 2026}}</ref>
